weeks.title: Foundations of Health Informatics
weeks.description: What health informatics is, interdisciplinary perspectives, and the health-data life cycle.
weeks.arDescription: مفهوم المعلوماتية الصحية وتكامل التخصصات ودورة حياة البيانات الصحية.

slides.title: Foundations of Health Informatics Weeks 1-2 study deck Introduction to health informatics, the health-data life cycle, DIKW, interdisciplinary skills, and data acumen
Learning outcomes
points: Define health informatics and explain its purpose in healthcare.
Describe the main stages of the health-data life cycle.
Explain why health data are complex and difficult to use.
Distinguish data, information, knowledge, and wisdom.
Explain the interdisciplinary skills and data acumen required in health informatics.

slides.title: WEEK 1 Health informatics and the health-data life cycle Focus: what health informatics is, why healthcare needs it, and how health data move from collection to use. Study goal: explain the field in your own words and describe each stage of the data life cycle.
What is health informatics?
points: Health informatics is an interdisciplinary field that connects health sciences, information sciences, and management sciences.
It is concerned with acquiring, managing, representing, and transforming health data.
Its purpose is to turn data into useful knowledge that can support healthcare decisions, interventions, and processes.
The field studies both technology and the people and workflows that use the technology.

slides.title: The central purpose of the field
points: Healthcare produces data during registration, assessment, diagnosis, treatment, monitoring, payment, and research.
Raw data are not automatically useful; they must be organized, interpreted, and placed in context.
Health informatics helps make the right information available to the right people at the right time.
The final goal is better decisions and improved health, not technology for its own sake.

slides.title: Why health informatics matters
points: Patient care depends on accurate and accessible information.
Healthcare professionals must coordinate across departments, organizations, and locations.
Digital systems can reduce delays, support safer decisions, and make patterns easier to identify.
Poorly managed information can lead to duplication, misunderstanding, delay, and risk to patients.
Health informatics connects information work with practical healthcare improvement.

slides.title: Health informatics is interdisciplinary
points: Health sciences contribute knowledge of patients, clinical care, health systems, terminology, and healthcare standards.
Information sciences contribute computing, databases, information retrieval, privacy, security, and human- computer interaction.
Management sciences contribute project management, quality improvement, finance, workflow, and organizational change.
Health informatics combines these perspectives because healthcare problems are rarely solved by one discipline alone.

slides.title: Contribution of health sciences
points: Understanding the healthcare system and how care is delivered.
Recognizing clinical information needs and the meaning of health data.
Using healthcare vocabulary, terminology, classification systems, and standards.
Understanding clinical workflows and the consequences of incomplete or incorrect information.
Keeping patient care and health outcomes at the center of informatics work.

slides.title: Contribution of information sciences
points: Designing and managing databases and information systems.
Retrieving, integrating, processing, and analyzing health data.
Protecting health information through privacy and security practices.
Designing usable systems through human-computer interaction.
Supporting communication between systems and users.

slides.title: Contribution of management sciences
points: Planning and managing health-information projects.
Improving processes, quality, efficiency, and patient safety.
Managing organizational change when new systems are introduced.
Considering financial, legal, ethical, and governance responsibilities.
Ensuring that technology fits the organization and its goals.

slides.title: Where the disciplines meet
points: Digital health interventions combine clinical needs, technology, and implementation planning.
Health-data governance combines data management with ethical, legal, and organizational responsibility.
Quality improvement combines healthcare knowledge, reliable data, and process management.
Legal and ethical issues in health IT require both technical understanding and professional judgment.
Successful informatics work depends on communication across professional groups.

slides.title: Health informatics and health IT
points: Health information technology refers mainly to the digital tools and systems used in healthcare.
Examples include electronic health records, laboratory systems, patient portals, and mobile-health applications.
Health informatics is broader: it examines how data, people, processes, and technology work together.
A system may function technically but still fail if it does not fit clinical workflow or user needs.
Technology is a tool; informatics focuses on meaningful and responsible use.

slides.title: Health informatics and health data science
points: Health data science focuses on transforming health data into knowledge that can support decisions.
It may use statistics, computing, analytical models, machine learning, and visualization.
Health informatics includes health data science but has a wider scope.
Health informatics also asks how knowledge will be used to create interventions, tools, and improved healthcare processes.
Data science produces insight; informatics connects insight with practice.

slides.title: How the field has evolved
points: Healthcare information moved from mainly paper records toward increasingly digital records and systems.
Separate departmental systems expanded into organization-wide electronic health records.
Greater connectivity increased the need for information exchange and shared standards.
Growth in digital data, analytics, and data science expanded the skills expected in health informatics.
The field continues to evolve as new data sources and digital-health tools appear.

slides.title: Main drivers of health informatics
points: Rapid growth in the volume and variety of health data.
Wider use of electronic records and connected healthcare systems.
Need for safer, higher-quality, and more coordinated care.
Demand for evidence-based decisions and measurable outcomes.
Need to manage cost, efficiency, privacy, security, and accountability.
Development of analytics, mobile health, and data-science methods.

slides.title: Why health data are complex
points: Health data describe people, conditions, treatments, behaviors, organizations, and outcomes.
They may be numerical, coded, written, spoken, imaged, measured by devices, or generated by patients.
Their meaning often depends on clinical context, time, place, and purpose.
More data types continue to appear as healthcare technologies develop.
Complexity makes careful management and interpretation essential.

slides.title: Structured and unstructured data
points: Structured data follow a defined format and are usually stored in specific fields.
Examples: age, laboratory value, diagnosis code, medication dose, and appointment date.
Unstructured data do not follow a simple fixed field structure.
Examples: clinical notes, discharge summaries, images, audio, and free-text patient messages.
Healthcare systems often need to combine both types to understand the full patient story.

slides.title: The semantic gap
points: A semantic gap occurs when the recorded data and the intended clinical meaning do not match clearly.
The same term may be used differently by different people or systems.
Abbreviations, local wording, missing context, and inconsistent coding can create confusion.
A number alone may be meaningless without the unit, time, method, and patient context.
Terminologies, standards, documentation rules, and human review help reduce the gap.

slides.title: Health data are distributed
points: A patient's information may be stored in clinics, hospitals, laboratories, pharmacies, imaging systems, and personal devices.
Each location may use different formats, definitions, and access rules.
Important information can be incomplete when systems do not communicate.
Linking data can improve continuity of care but also creates privacy, security, and governance responsibilities.
Health informatics addresses both access to data and trustworthy use of data.

slides.title: The health-data life cycle
points: The life cycle describes how health data move through a series of connected stages.
A useful introductory sequence is: create or collect; store; manage and standardize; analyze; communicate and use; retain or dispose.
Data quality, privacy, security, governance, and ethics apply throughout the entire cycle.
A problem at an early stage can affect every later stage.
The cycle repeats as new observations and decisions create more data.

slides.title: Stage 1: create or collect data
points: Data are created during care, administration, monitoring, research, and patient activities.
Examples include vital signs, diagnoses, medication orders, clinical notes, images, claims, and wearable- device readings.
Collection may be manual, entered into a form, imported from another system, or captured automatically by a device.
Clear definitions and accurate entry are important because later use depends on what is captured now.

slides.title: Stage 2: store and protect data
points: Data are stored in records, databases, repositories, and connected information systems.
Storage should preserve accuracy, availability, confidentiality, and appropriate access.
Organizations decide who may view, enter, correct, or share different types of information.
Backups, security controls, and reliable system operation help prevent loss or unauthorized use.
Storage is not only technical; it is also a governance responsibility.

slides.title: Stage 3: manage and standardize data
points: Data are checked, cleaned, organized, coded, and prepared for use.
Standard terms and formats help different users and systems interpret information consistently.
Duplicate, missing, incorrect, or conflicting entries should be identified.
Metadata provide information about the data, such as source, date, unit, and method.
Good management reduces ambiguity and improves later retrieval and analysis.

slides.title: Stage 4: analyze and interpret data
points: Analysis looks for summaries, comparisons, trends, relationships, and patterns.
The method must match the question and the quality of the available data.
Results require interpretation within clinical and organizational context.
An analytical result can be mathematically correct but still misleading if the source data or assumptions are poor.
Health data science contributes many methods used at this stage.

slides.title: Stage 5: communicate and use information
points: Findings may be communicated through the EHR, reports, alerts, dashboards, visualizations, or conversations.
Information should be understandable, relevant, timely, and appropriate for the intended user.
Clinicians, managers, patients, researchers, and public-health teams may need different presentations of the same data.
Use may lead to a clinical decision, process change, policy, intervention, or new research question.
This stage connects information with action.

slides.title: Stage 6: retain or dispose of data
points: Some health data must be kept for clinical, legal, administrative, or research purposes.
Retention rules determine what is kept, for how long, and under whose responsibility.
Data that are no longer needed should be disposed of securely and according to policy.
Archived data must remain protected and retrievable when required.
Responsible disposal reduces unnecessary risk while preserving required information.

slides.title: Life-cycle example: a laboratory result
points: Create: a blood sample is tested and a result is produced.
Store: the result is saved in the laboratory system and patient record.
Manage: patient identity, test name, unit, reference range, date, and status are verified.
Analyze: the result is compared with reference values and earlier results.
Communicate and use: the clinician reviews it and decides whether action is needed.
Retain: the result remains part of the patient's longitudinal record.

slides.title: Week 1 summary
points: Health informatics connects health sciences, information sciences, and management sciences.
Its central work is transforming health data into useful knowledge and improved healthcare action.
Health data are complex because they are varied, contextual, distributed, and partly unstructured.
The health-data life cycle links collection, storage, management, analysis, use, retention, and disposal.
People, processes, technology, standards, governance, and ethics influence every stage.

weeks.title: From Data to Knowledge and Wisdom
weeks.description: DIKW, data literacy, data acumen, and informed decisions.
weeks.arDescription: هرم البيانات والمعلومات والمعرفة والحكمة ومهارات فهم البيانات واتخاذ القرار.

slides.title: WEEK 2 From data to knowledge and wisdom Focus: how raw facts gain meaning and become a basis for decisions and action. Study goal: distinguish all four DIKW levels and explain data literacy, data acumen, and core informatics competencies.
The DIKW framework
points: DIKW stands for data, information, knowledge, and wisdom.
The framework explains how raw observations can be transformed into meaningful and useful understanding.
Each level adds value through context, connection, interpretation, or application.
Moving upward is not automatic; it requires sound methods and human judgment.
In healthcare, the purpose is to support safe and appropriate action.

slides.title: Data: raw facts
points: Data are discrete, unorganized, raw, and objective facts recorded from observations or transactions.
Examples include 39.1 degrees Celsius, heart rate 120, age 67, or a recorded medication dose.
A data value may have little meaning without a label, unit, date, source, or patient context.
Accurate data collection is the foundation of the remaining DIKW levels.
Poor data cannot reliably produce good information.

slides.title: Information: data with context
points: Information is data that have been organized, structured, and placed in context.
The value 39.1 becomes information when identified as a patient's oral temperature measured at 10:00 a.m.
Context helps answer basic questions such as who, what, when, where, and how.
Labels, units, reference ranges, patient identity, and time can transform a value into meaningful information.
Information is useful only when its context is accurate.

slides.title: Knowledge: connected information
points: Knowledge forms when related information is connected and patterns are understood.
A temperature of 39.1, increased heart rate, symptoms, and laboratory findings may together indicate a clinical problem.
Knowledge explains relationships and supports understanding of what the information may mean.
Clinical knowledge, guidelines, prior experience, and analytical evidence may contribute.
Knowledge is more than a collection of separate facts.

slides.title: Wisdom: applying knowledge
points: Wisdom is the appropriate application of knowledge to solve a problem or choose an action.
It requires judgment about the patient, evidence, risks, benefits, values, and available options.
A decision should not be based on a single data point without context.
Technology may support a decision, but professional responsibility remains important.
Informatics is valuable when knowledge is translated into effective practice.

slides.title: DIKW example: birth weight
points: Data: a baby's recorded birth weight.
Information: birth weight combined with the mother's age, race, residence, and other context.
Knowledge: a pattern showing that low birth weight is associated with socioeconomic conditions.
Wisdom: using the knowledge to design and target an appropriate maternal-health program.
The example shows how value increases as context, relationships, and action are added.

slides.title: DIKW example: hospital readmission
points: Data: discharge date, diagnosis, medications, follow-up date, and return admission.
Information: readmission rates organized by condition, unit, and time period.
Knowledge: patients without timely follow-up show a higher pattern of readmission.
Wisdom: the organization introduces targeted follow-up and monitors whether outcomes improve.
The decision should still consider data quality, fairness, feasibility, and patient needs.

slides.title: Transformation requires work
points: Data must be captured correctly before they can be trusted.
Organization and context are needed to create information.
Comparison, connection, and interpretation are needed to create knowledge.
Judgment and responsibility are needed to apply knowledge wisely.
Errors, bias, missing context, or misunderstanding at any stage can lead to poor decisions.

slides.title: Data literacy
points: Data literacy is the ability to read, understand, work with, and communicate about data.
A data-literate person asks where the data came from and what each value represents.
They check definitions, units, completeness, limitations, and appropriate interpretation.
They can explain findings clearly without overstating what the data prove.
Data literacy is a critical skill in healthcare and health informatics.

slides.title: Data acumen
points: Data acumen is the ability to make good judgments about using data to support evidence-based decisions.
It extends beyond technical data-management skills.
It includes deciding whether data are suitable, methods are appropriate, and conclusions are justified.
It also includes understanding workflow, communication, governance, and ethical consequences.
A person may know how to analyze data but still need acumen to use the result responsibly.

slides.title: Main areas of data acumen
points: Foundations: basic statistics, computing, and understanding of evidence.
Data management: database design, storage, retrieval, and organization.
Data preparation: cleaning and transforming data for analysis.
Analysis: analytical modeling, machine learning, and interpretation.
Practice: healthcare workflow, reproducibility, communication, visualization, governance, and ethics.

slides.title: Questions for sound data use
points: Purpose: What decision or problem is this data intended to support?
Meaning: How were the variables defined and measured?
Quality: Are important values missing, incorrect, delayed, or inconsistent?
Representativeness: Which patients or settings are included or excluded?
Interpretation: Does the evidence support the conclusion being made?
Action: What are the possible benefits, harms, ethical issues, and monitoring needs?

slides.title: Core competencies in health informatics
points: Understand healthcare systems, workflows, vocabulary, terminology, classifications, and standards.
Manage data through databases, retrieval, integration, preparation, and analysis.
Support privacy, security, legal compliance, ethical practice, and data governance.
Use project management, quality improvement, communication, and visualization skills.
Work effectively across clinical, technical, administrative, research, and patient perspectives.

slides.title: Key terms to know
points: Health informatics: use of health data, information, knowledge, people, processes, and technology to improve healthcare.
Health data science: methods that transform health data into knowledge for decision-making.
Semantic gap: difference between recorded data and the meaning intended or understood.
DIKW: data, information, knowledge, and wisdom.
Data literacy: ability to understand and communicate with data.
Data acumen: ability to make sound judgments about the use of data.

slides.title: Common misunderstandings
points: Health informatics is not only computers; it includes people, processes, information, and decisions.
More data do not automatically create better knowledge; quality and context still matter.
A dashboard does not make a decision; people must interpret and apply its information.
Health data science is part of health informatics, not the whole field.
Technical skill alone is not enough; ethical, clinical, organizational, and communication judgment are also required.

slides.title: Study questions
points: Define health informatics in your own words and state its main purpose.
Why is health informatics described as an interdisciplinary field?
How is health informatics broader than health data science?
List the stages of the health-data life cycle and explain why they are connected.
Give one healthcare example for each DIKW level.
What is the difference between data literacy and data acumen?

slides.title: Final summary
points: Health informatics transforms health data into knowledge and action by connecting healthcare, information, and management disciplines.
Health data require careful collection, storage, management, analysis, communication, retention, and disposal.
The DIKW framework explains how raw facts gain context, form patterns, and guide responsible decisions.
Data literacy supports understanding; data acumen supports sound judgment.
The ultimate measure of informatics is whether information is used safely, ethically, and effectively to improve health and healthcare.

weeks.title: Electronic Health Records
weeks.description: EHR foundations, clinical and administrative functions, and connected care.
weeks.arDescription: أسس السجلات الصحية الإلكترونية والوظائف السريرية والإدارية والرعاية المتصلة.

slides.title: Electronic Health Records and Clinical Information Systems Weeks 3 EHR foundations, clinical and administrative functions, care settings, patient access, and introductory clinical decision support
Learning outcomes
points: Define an electronic health record and explain its purpose.
Describe the historical development and major functions of EHRs.
Distinguish clinical, administrative, primary, and secondary uses of EHR data.
Compare inpatient, ambulatory, long-term-care, and personal health records.
Explain how clinical information systems and decision support contribute to patient care.

slides.title: WEEK 3 EHR foundations and connected clinical systems Focus: what an EHR is, how it developed, what it contains, and how major clinical and administrative systems contribute to the record. Study goal: explain the main EHR functions and trace how information moves across connected healthcare systems.
What is an electronic health record?
points: An electronic health record, or EHR, is a digital record of health information used across time and healthcare services.
It brings together clinical and administrative information needed to support care.
Authorized users can enter, retrieve, review, update, and share information according to their roles.
An EHR supports individual patient care and wider organizational activities.
The value of an EHR depends on accurate data, usable design, appropriate access, and reliable workflow.

slides.title: What an EHR may contain
points: Patient identification and demographic information.
Problems, diagnoses, allergies, medications, immunizations, and health history.
Clinical notes, care plans, orders, results, procedures, and discharge information.
Appointments, insurance information, authorizations, claims, and payments.
Patient messages, educational materials, reminders, and information from connected systems.

slides.title: Why health records became electronic
points: Healthcare organizations needed more timely access to patient information.
Safety concerns increased interest in automation, standardized entry, and electronic checking.
Departments such as laboratory, radiology, and pharmacy required specialized digital systems.
Organizations wanted information to support care, billing, reporting, quality improvement, and research.
Growing connectivity created an expectation that information could follow patients across services.

slides.title: Early development of EHR systems
points: During the 1980s, many vendor systems focused on the needs of individual ancillary departments.
Laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, and procedure areas often developed separate electronic functions.
During the 1990s, development moved toward broader electronic patient records.
The goal gradually shifted from automating one department to connecting information across the organization.
This history explains why some healthcare organizations still use many separate systems.

slides.title: Connected care became the next goal
points: In the early 2000s, internet capabilities supported wider access and communication.
EHR deployment expanded across hospitals, physician offices, and long-term-care settings.
The need to exchange information between different systems made interoperability increasingly important.
Health information exchanges and personal health records developed to extend access beyond one EHR.
Telehealth and consumer expectations later increased demand for remote and patient-facing services.

slides.title: A selected U.S. policy milestone
points: The 2009 HITECH Act created incentives for eligible U.S. physicians and hospitals to adopt certified EHR technology.
Programs linked EHR capabilities and use with federal payment requirements.
Later rules emphasized access, information sharing, and price transparency.
This is one national example of how policy can accelerate adoption and influence system design.
Specific laws and requirements differ between countries and healthcare systems.

slides.title: EHRs are used in different settings
points: Inpatient EHRs support care during hospital admission and across hospital departments.
Ambulatory EHRs support outpatient visits before, during, and after the encounter.
Long-term-care EHRs support continuing care, minimum data requirements, and communication with hospitals.
Personal health records and patient portals give patients access to selected information and services.
The core purpose is similar, but workflows and information needs differ by setting.

slides.title: Clinical and administrative functions
points: Clinical functions directly support assessment, diagnosis, treatment, monitoring, and communication about care.
Administrative functions support scheduling, authorization, claims, payment, inventory, and organizational operations.
The two groups are connected; a clinical service can create documentation, supply use, billing, and reporting data.
Well-integrated systems reduce repeated entry and help information flow between care and operations.
Users should understand why information is recorded and who needs it later.

slides.title: Primary and secondary uses
points: Primary use means using information directly to provide and coordinate care for a patient.
Examples include reviewing history, entering orders, documenting services, and monitoring results.
Secondary use means using information for another legitimate purpose beyond the immediate encounter.
Examples include quality improvement, population health, billing, research, education, and planning.
Secondary use requires attention to data quality, privacy, access, and appropriate interpretation.

slides.title: Clinical documentation
points: Different healthcare professionals document assessments, observations, diagnoses, interventions, and outcomes.
Documentation creates a shared account of what happened and why decisions were made.
Complete and timely notes support communication, continuity of care, safety, billing, and legal requirements.
Templates and structured fields can improve consistency but may not capture every clinical detail.
Free text can add context but may be harder to search and analyze.

slides.title: Orders and results
points: Authorized clinicians can place orders for laboratory tests, imaging, procedures, and other services.
Orders are transmitted to the department responsible for completing the service.
Results return to the EHR for review, interpretation, and follow-up.
Electronic status information can show whether an order is pending, completed, corrected, or cancelled.
Clear links between the order, result, patient, time, and responsible professional support safety.

slides.title: Medication management and e-prescribing
points: Medication orders can move electronically from the clinician to pharmacy systems.
E-prescribing sends outpatient prescriptions to a pharmacy and may check insurance formulary information.
The EHR may check allergies, duplicate therapy, dose, interactions, and other safety rules.
In hospitals, electronic orders can connect with pharmacy verification and medication administration.
Alerts support users but do not replace professional review and patient assessment.

slides.title: Prevention and chronic-care support
points: EHRs can record immunizations and identify preventive services that are due.
Registries organize information about groups of patients with conditions such as diabetes.
Reminders may support screening, vaccination, monitoring, or follow-up.
Templates help collect consistent information over repeated visits.
Patient education can be selected and sent through the EHR or patient portal.

slides.title: Administrative functions
points: Schedule visits, procedures, tests, staff, rooms, and equipment.
Verify insurance coverage and manage pre-authorization requirements.
Generate and submit claims using information recorded during care.
Connect supply use with scheduled and completed procedures.
Support online payment and other patient financial services.
Provide operational reports for managers and departments.

slides.title: Community and population functions
points: Population-health tools summarize information across groups rather than one patient at a time.
Immunization programs use records to identify coverage and gaps.
Research and clinical-trial activities may use appropriately governed EHR data.
Interoperable connections can link hospitals with community, retail, and virtual-care providers.
Remote monitoring can extend support to rural or high-risk populations.

slides.title: Clinical information systems
points: A clinical information system supports a particular area of patient care or clinical work.
Examples include laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, cardiology, and procedure systems.
These systems may create detailed information that becomes part of the wider EHR.
Users may work within the specialized system, the EHR, or both.
Integration is important so that orders, results, status, and patient identity remain consistent.

slides.title: Laboratory information system
points: Receives laboratory orders and identifies the patient and requested tests.
Supports specimen collection, labeling, tracking, testing, verification, and reporting.
Sends verified results to the EHR for clinician review.
May flag results outside the reference range or results requiring urgent communication.
Correct patient identification, units, reference ranges, and result status are essential.

slides.title: Radiology systems and PACS
points: Radiology information systems support imaging orders, scheduling, workflow, and reports.
A picture archiving and communication system, or PACS, stores and displays medical images.
The EHR may provide access to the radiology report and a link to the images.
Integration connects the correct order, patient, examination, image, and interpretation.
Examples include X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound, and other diagnostic imaging.

slides.title: Pharmacy information system
points: Receives medication orders and supports pharmacist review and preparation.
Maintains information about medications, doses, schedules, and dispensing.
Can exchange information with the EHR, medication-administration tools, and billing systems.
Safety checks may include allergies, interactions, duplicate therapy, and dose concerns.
Clinical judgment remains necessary when interpreting warnings and patient circumstances.

slides.title: Integration creates a shared record
points: The EHR acts as a central access point, while specialized systems perform detailed departmental work.
An order entered once should reach the correct system without unnecessary repeated entry.
A completed result should return to the correct patient record and responsible user.
Interfaces and shared standards help systems exchange information.
Breakdowns in identity, meaning, timing, or status can create clinical and administrative risk.

slides.title: Week 3 summary
points: An EHR is a longitudinal digital record that supports clinical and administrative work.
EHRs developed from separate departmental systems toward connected records and services.
Clinical functions include documentation, orders, results, medications, prevention, and patient education.
Administrative functions include scheduling, authorization, claims, inventory, payment, and reporting.
Laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, and other systems contribute information to the shared record.

weeks.title: EHR Workflows & Decision Support
weeks.description: Inpatient and outpatient workflows, CPOE, personal records, and decision support.
weeks.arDescription: سير عمل المستشفيات والعيادات وإدخال أوامر مقدمي الرعاية ودعم القرار.

slides.title: WEEK 4 EHR use across care settings and decision support Focus: how EHR workflows differ in hospitals, outpatient care, long-term care, and patient-facing records. Study goal: compare the settings and explain how computerized ordering and decision support can improve care while creating new risks.
Inpatient EHR
points: An inpatient EHR supports care during admission to a hospital or similar facility.
Many professionals use the same record across shifts, units, and departments.
The record supports admission, assessment, orders, medication administration, procedures, progress notes, and discharge.
Information changes rapidly, so current status, responsibility, and communication are important.
Hospital safety functions often connect bedside care with laboratory, radiology, and pharmacy systems.

slides.title: Computerized provider order entry
points: Computerized provider order entry, or CPOE, allows authorized providers to enter orders electronically.
Orders can be sent directly to pharmacy, laboratory, radiology, or other departments.
Standard order choices improve consistency and legibility.
Required fields can reduce incomplete orders.
Rules may generate alerts or reminders related to safety, policy, or cost.

slides.title: CPOE and medication safety
points: Electronic medication orders can connect prescribing, pharmacy review, dispensing, and administration.
Patient identification technologies such as barcodes or RFID may support bedside verification.
The system can compare the medication order with allergies, dose ranges, interactions, and formulary information.
The purpose is to reduce preventable errors and improve consistency.
Technology supports safety only when users follow reliable workflows and respond appropriately.

slides.title: Inpatient EHR adoption develops in stages
points: Early implementation focuses on technical infrastructure and reliable electronic data.
Later development adds documentation, medication functions, CPOE, and stronger safety capabilities.
More advanced stages connect the hospital record with patients and external organizations.
The exact maturity model may vary, but the general idea is gradual development rather than one-time installation.
Adoption includes people, workflow, training, governance, and continuous improvement.

slides.title: Ambulatory EHR
points: An ambulatory EHR supports outpatient clinics and focuses on a visit or episode of care.
It assists activities before, during, and after the visit.
Clinical and administrative functions are closely connected around the appointment.
Information may flow to a hospital EHR when the same organization or compatible systems are used.
Different vendor systems may exchange information through a health information exchange.

slides.title: Before the outpatient visit
points: The patient schedules the visit online, by telephone, or through staff.
Insurance and authorization information may be checked before arrival.
The patient may update demographics, medications, symptoms, history, and forms through a portal.
The care team can review previous problems, tests, and planned follow-up.
Good preparation reduces repeated entry and supports efficient use of visit time.

slides.title: During the outpatient visit
points: Staff document observations, history, assessment, diagnosis, and the care plan.
The clinician may order tests, medications, referrals, or procedures.
E-prescribing can send medication orders to a selected pharmacy.
Decision-support reminders may identify preventive or chronic-care needs.
The encounter documentation supports communication, follow-up, and billing.

slides.title: After the outpatient visit
points: The patient receives an after-visit summary and instructions.
Results may become available with the provider's interpretation.
The system can send health-maintenance reminders and educational content.
Secure messaging supports questions and communication with the provider's office.
Patients can schedule follow-up visits, testing, or procedures.
The record preserves historical problems, allergies, tests, and visits.

slides.title: Inpatient and ambulatory EHRs
points: Inpatient care covers continuous care during admission; ambulatory care focuses on scheduled visits or episodes.
Inpatient records change frequently across shifts and departments; ambulatory records emphasize longitudinal follow-up between visits.
Hospitals often require intensive order, medication, procedure, and discharge workflows.
Outpatient systems emphasize scheduling, pre-visit information, e-prescribing, results, reminders, and messaging.
Both settings need accurate identification, documentation, communication, security, and continuity.

slides.title: Long-term-care EHR
points: Long-term-care EHRs support residents who receive ongoing care over extended periods.
They may use specialized vendor systems designed for long-term-care workflows.
The record supports a core minimum data set, care planning, medication information, assessments, and communication.
Digital exchange with hospitals is important when residents are transferred between settings.
Continuity depends on timely and accurate information during transitions of care.

slides.title: Personal health record
points: A personal health record, or PHR, is related to the EHR but is designed for access and use by the individual.
It may allow a person to view health information and manage selected health activities.
PHRs can support appointments, results, messages, reminders, payments, education, and personal data entry.
Patients may authorize another person to manage the record by proxy.
A PHR does not replace the provider's legal clinical record.

slides.title: Tethered and untethered PHRs
points: A tethered PHR is connected to an organization's EHR and shares data or functions with it.
A patient portal is a common example of a tethered PHR function.
An untethered PHR is a stand-alone record managed separately from a provider's EHR.
Tethered records may update automatically from the healthcare organization.
Untethered records may give the person broader control but require manual entry or separate connections.

slides.title: PHR benefits for patients
points: Schedule appointments using web or mobile services.
View results, selected record information, and provider interpretations.
Receive reminders and educational material.
Send secure messages and complete information before a visit.
Pay bills and review authorization information.
Add information and manage another person's record by proxy with consent.

slides.title: PHR benefits for organizations
points: Patients can complete routine tasks such as scheduling, messaging, results review, and bill payment online.
Patients may add useful information about over-the-counter medicines or care received elsewhere.
Digital services can support chronic-disease management and remote monitoring.
Virtual visits can extend access and help organizations offer convenient services.
Benefits depend on usability, accessibility, consent, workflow, and staff capacity to respond.

slides.title: Patient portals support engagement
points: A portal gives patients a secure digital route to selected health information and services.
Access can help patients prepare for visits, understand results, follow instructions, and participate in decisions.
Secure messaging can improve communication but requires clear response expectations.
Digital access must consider language, disability, health literacy, internet access, and digital skills.
Proxy access and consent are important when caregivers assist another person.

slides.title: Clinical decision support
points: A clinical decision support system, or CDSS, provides patient-specific or situation-specific information to support a healthcare decision.
Examples include medication warnings, preventive-care reminders, order guidance, and prompts for missing information.
Decision support may be integrated into the EHR workflow.
It can improve consistency, safety, quality, and access to relevant knowledge.
The clinician remains responsible for interpreting the information and deciding what action is appropriate.

slides.title: The five rights of decision support
points: The right information: relevant and evidence-based content.
To the right person: the user responsible for the decision or action.
In the right format: alert, order set, reminder, reference, or another usable form.
Through the right channel: within the EHR, portal, mobile system, report, or communication process.
At the right time: early enough to influence the decision without causing unnecessary interruption.

slides.title: Preventive-care reminders
points: The EHR can compare patient information with rules for screening, vaccination, and chronic-care monitoring.
A reminder may show what is due, the due date, and the most recent completion date.
Examples include influenza vaccination, colon-cancer screening, cholesterol monitoring, and diabetic eye examination.
The user must confirm whether the information is complete and relevant to the individual patient.
A reminder supports action but does not automatically determine the correct care.

slides.title: Benefits and limitations of CDSS
points: Potential benefits include timely knowledge, standardized practice, prevention, safer orders, and fewer missed actions.
Poorly designed alerts can interrupt workflow and contribute to alert fatigue.
Incorrect, incomplete, delayed, or biased data can produce inappropriate recommendations.
Users may over-rely on the system or ignore useful warnings after repeated low-value alerts.
Good decision support requires evidence, testing, usability, leadership, monitoring, and regular improvement.

slides.title: A connected patient journey
points: Before care: the patient schedules through the portal and updates information.
During the visit: the clinician documents findings and enters laboratory and medication orders.
Across systems: laboratory and pharmacy systems receive the orders and return status or results.
Decision support: the EHR displays a relevant warning or preventive reminder.
After care: the patient receives instructions, results, messages, and follow-up reminders.
Over time: the shared record supports continuity, quality review, and population-level learning.

slides.title: Key terms to know
points: EHR: longitudinal digital health record used across healthcare services.
Clinical information system: specialized system supporting a clinical department or function.
CPOE: electronic entry and transmission of provider orders.
E-prescribing: electronic transmission of prescriptions to a pharmacy.
PHR: personal record or access tool designed for the individual.
Patient portal: secure patient-facing connection to an organization's EHR.
CDSS: system that provides relevant information to support decisions.

slides.title: Study questions
points: What is an EHR, and why is it more than a digital copy of a paper chart?
Distinguish clinical functions from administrative functions.
What is the difference between primary and secondary use of EHR data?
How do laboratory, radiology, and pharmacy systems contribute to the EHR?
Compare inpatient, ambulatory, long-term-care, and personal health records.
What are the five rights of clinical decision support?
Give one benefit and one possible unintended consequence of CDSS.

slides.title: Final summary
points: EHRs organize longitudinal clinical and administrative information to support care and healthcare operations.
Specialized laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, and other systems contribute detailed information to the shared record.
Workflows differ across inpatient, ambulatory, long-term-care, and patient-facing settings.
CPOE, portals, e-prescribing, and decision support can improve access, coordination, safety, and engagement.
Technology works well only when data are accurate and the system fits users, workflow, policy, ethics, and patient needs.

weeks.title: Health Information Exchange
weeks.description: Continuity of care, health information exchange, and interoperability.
weeks.arDescription: استمرارية الرعاية وتبادل المعلومات الصحية والتشغيل البيني.

slides.title: Health Information Exchange, Interoperability and Data Standards Weeks 5 Why health information must move across care settings and how shared standards preserve its meaning
Learning outcomes
points: Explain health information exchange and its role in continuity of care.
Distinguish the exchange process from an organization that manages exchange.
Explain interoperability in clear, nontechnical language.
Recognize ICD, SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm, HL7, and FHIR and state their main purposes.
Discuss common benefits, barriers, consent questions, and public-health uses of exchange.

slides.title: WEEK 5 Health information exchange and interoperability Focus: why information must follow patients across organizations, professions, and care settings. Study goal: explain the exchange process, its benefits, and the conditions needed for information to be useful and trusted.
Healthcare information must travel
points: A patient may receive care from clinics, hospitals, laboratories, pharmacies, imaging centers, and other organizations.
Each setting may create a separate part of the patient's health history.
Care becomes fragmented when important information remains inside one system.
Electronic exchange helps authorized users obtain relevant information when and where it is needed.
The goal is better continuity, not the transfer of every available data element.

slides.title: What health information exchange means
points: Health information exchange, or HIE, is the electronic sharing of health information between authorized participants.
Participants may include healthcare providers, laboratories, pharmacies, public-health agencies, and patients.
Exchange can occur directly between two organizations or through a wider network.
HIE supports access to information created outside the user's own organization.
Successful exchange requires technology, standards, governance, trust, and usable workflows.

slides.title: HIE and HIO are related but different
points: HIE can describe the process of electronically sharing health information.
A health information organization, or HIO, is an entity that facilitates or manages exchange.
An HIO may establish participation rules, identity processes, privacy protections, and technical services.
Not every exchange requires a separate HIO; organizations may exchange information directly.
The distinction helps separate the activity of exchange from the organization that supports it.

slides.title: Many participants contribute to exchange
points: Hospitals contribute admissions, diagnoses, procedures, discharge summaries, and results.
Clinics contribute encounter notes, medication lists, referrals, and follow-up plans.
Laboratories and imaging services contribute orders, results, reports, and status information.
Pharmacies contribute medication-dispensing information and support medication reconciliation.
Public-health agencies may receive reportable-condition data and return alerts or guidance.

slides.title: Continuity of care is the main purpose
points: Continuity means that relevant information remains available as the patient moves between care settings.
The next provider can understand recent diagnoses, treatments, medicines, allergies, tests, and plans.
Accessible information can reduce repeated history taking and unnecessary duplicate testing.
Timely exchange supports safer referrals, transfers, discharge, and follow-up.
Information must still be reviewed in the context of the current patient encounter.

slides.title: A patient journey shows why exchange matters
points: A patient visits a clinic, where the clinician identifies a problem and orders laboratory testing.
The laboratory completes the test and returns a standardized result.
The patient is later admitted to a hospital that needs the clinic history and laboratory result.
After discharge, the clinic needs the hospital diagnosis, medication changes, and follow-up plan.
HIE connects these episodes so each authorized care team can work from a more complete history.

slides.title: A summary of care supports transitions
points: A summary of care communicates essential information when a patient is referred or transferred.
Common elements include current problems, medicines, allergies, procedures, and laboratory information.
Demographic information and provider details help identify the patient and responsible care team.
A care plan can clarify goals, instructions, and required follow-up.
The receiving team must confirm that the information is current, complete, and clinically relevant.

slides.title: Patients can benefit from connected information
points: Patients may avoid repeating the same history and tests at every organization.
Care teams can identify allergies, recent results, and medication changes more quickly.
Transitions may become safer because the next provider has more context.
Electronic access can help patients view, download, or transmit selected health information.
Benefits depend on accurate identity matching, meaningful consent, and protection of sensitive information.

slides.title: Providers can make better-informed decisions
points: External records can provide information that is unavailable in the local EHR.
Previous tests and treatments may help the clinician avoid unnecessary repetition.
A broader medication history may support safer prescribing and reconciliation.
Information from other settings can improve treatment planning and communication with patients.
Too much poorly organized information can also increase workload, so usability remains important.

slides.title: Organizations and communities also benefit
points: Exchange can support coordination across hospitals, clinics, laboratories, pharmacies, and community services.
Shared information may reduce avoidable duplication and improve operational efficiency.
Aggregated information can support quality measurement and population-health planning.
Public-health reporting can become faster and more complete.
Benefits may be distributed across many stakeholders, making funding and sustainability difficult.

slides.title: Interoperability goes beyond connectivity
points: Interoperability is the ability of different systems to connect, exchange information, and use it in a coordinated way.
Connectivity only means that systems can send or receive data.
Useful exchange also requires a shared structure and a shared understanding of meaning.
Information must arrive in the correct patient record and fit the receiving workflow.
Interoperability is successful when exchanged information supports appropriate action.

slides.title: Exchange is not automatically interoperable
points: A scanned document can be exchanged, but its information may not be searchable or reusable.
A laboratory result may be transmitted, but a local code may have no meaning to the receiving system.
A medicine name may be written differently across organizations.
A technically successful message may still be incomplete, delayed, duplicated, or attached to the wrong patient.
Standards and quality controls help turn transmitted data into usable information.

slides.title: Technical barriers can interrupt exchange
points: Organizations may use different EHR products, interfaces, data formats, and technical capabilities.
Older systems may not support modern exchange functions.
Reliable patient matching is difficult when identifying information is missing or inconsistent.
Network availability, authentication, and system performance affect access.
Technical connection must be maintained, monitored, tested, and updated over time.

slides.title: Data differences can change meaning
points: The same clinical concept may be recorded with different words or local codes.
Information may be incomplete, outdated, duplicated, or recorded at different levels of detail.
Units, reference ranges, dates, and status values may differ between systems.
Mapping can translate local data to shared standards, but mapping also requires careful validation.
Consistent coding and documentation make exchanged information easier to interpret.

slides.title: Privacy, security, and trust are essential
points: Health information is sensitive and should be available only to authorized people for appropriate purposes.
Participants need rules for access, authentication, auditing, confidentiality, and secure transmission.
Patients and providers may resist exchange when they do not trust its protections or governance.
Sensitive information may require additional controls or segmentation.
Security protects exchange, while trust encourages people and organizations to participate.

slides.title: Consent models balance access and control
points: An opt-in model requires the patient to agree before information is included or shared.
An opt-out model includes information unless the patient chooses not to participate.
Some models allow restrictions on particular data, providers, or purposes.
More detailed choices can increase patient control but may be difficult to administer consistently.
Consent requirements depend on applicable law, policy, organization, data type, and care context.

slides.title: Workflow determines whether HIE is used
points: Information must be available during the clinical task, not after the decision has already been made.
Users need a clear way to locate, review, and incorporate outside information.
Too many documents or poorly organized data can create additional work.
Time pressure, staffing, training, and system usability influence adoption.
Successful HIE becomes part of normal care processes rather than a separate optional step.

slides.title: Centralized and federated exchange differ
points: A centralized, or aggregated, model combines participant data in a shared repository.
Participants query the repository for available patient information.
A federated model leaves detailed data with the original organizations.
A locator service helps identify where information exists, and the requesting organization retrieves it.
Each model involves tradeoffs in speed, complexity, control, privacy, security, and governance.

slides.title: HIE supports population and public health
points: Data from multiple care settings can help describe health patterns in a defined population.
Aggregated information can support prevention, quality improvement, and planning.
Electronic reporting can help public-health authorities identify notifiable conditions and outbreaks.
Exchange can support immunization reporting, surveillance, alerts, and disaster response.
These uses require standardized data, reliable quality, privacy protection, and appropriate governance.

slides.title: Exchange can follow different patterns
points: Directed exchange sends information to a known authorized recipient, such as during a referral.
Query-based exchange allows an authorized user to search for information held by participating organizations.
A shared repository can make selected information available through one exchange service.
Consumer-mediated exchange allows patients to obtain and transmit selected information.
The appropriate pattern depends on the use case, urgency, available systems, governance, and consent requirements.

slides.title: Week 5 summary
points: HIE electronically shares health information across authorized participants.
An HIO may provide the organization, rules, and services that support exchange.
Interoperability means that different systems can exchange and meaningfully use information.
HIE can improve continuity, coordination, decision-making, and public-health reporting.
Technology alone is insufficient; standards, quality, workflow, privacy, trust, and sustainability also matter.

weeks.title: Healthcare Data Standards
weeks.description: ICD, SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm, HL7, and FHIR.
weeks.arDescription: معايير تصنيف وترميز وتبادل البيانات الصحية مثل ICD وSNOMED CT وLOINC وFHIR.

slides.title: WEEK 6 Healthcare data standards Focus: how shared classifications, terminologies, identifiers, and exchange standards preserve meaning across systems. Study goal: recognize the main standards and explain what type of information each one supports.
Shared standards make data understandable
points: Healthcare contains many professions, organizations, systems, concepts, and local ways of recording information.
A standard provides an agreed way to represent, organize, or exchange information.
Standards reduce ambiguity when data move between people and systems.
They support consistent documentation, reporting, analysis, reimbursement, and decision support.
A standard does not guarantee good data; users must still document and apply it correctly.

slides.title: Different standards solve different problems
points: A vocabulary provides words or phrases and their meanings.
A terminology represents concepts within a clinical or technical domain.
A classification groups related conditions or activities into categories.
A code set assigns identifiers that systems can store and transmit.
An exchange standard defines how information is structured and communicated between systems.

slides.title: Classification and terminology are not the same
points: A classification organizes information into categories for reporting, statistics, reimbursement, or comparison.
A clinical terminology represents detailed concepts used in documentation and care.
Classifications often reduce detail so cases can be counted within consistent groups.
Terminologies often preserve greater clinical detail and relationships between concepts.
Mappings may connect a detailed terminology to a classification for secondary uses.

slides.title: ICD classifies diseases and health conditions
points: The International Classification of Diseases, or ICD, organizes diseases and health conditions into standardized categories.
It supports mortality and morbidity statistics, reporting, reimbursement, quality management, and research.
Health-record information is assigned to ICD categories according to applicable coding rules.
Aggregated ICD data help organizations and countries compare trends over time.
Students need to understand ICD's purpose, not memorize individual codes in this course.

slides.title: ICD data support many secondary uses
points: Public-health agencies use classified data to monitor diseases and causes of death.
Healthcare organizations use it for reporting, quality review, planning, and reimbursement.
Researchers use classified data to compare patient groups and health outcomes.
More specific classifications require more complete and precise clinical documentation.
Changes between ICD versions may require mapping and careful interpretation of historical data.

slides.title: ICD variants depend on purpose and setting
points: ICD is maintained internationally, while countries may adopt modifications or implementation rules.
Clinical modifications can provide additional detail for diagnosis reporting.
Some procedure classifications are designed for specific settings or national requirements.
The exact version and rules used should match the jurisdiction and reporting purpose.
The central idea remains consistent classification of health conditions for comparison and use.

slides.title: SNOMED CT represents detailed clinical concepts
points: SNOMED CT is a comprehensive clinical terminology used to represent health concepts in structured form.
It includes concepts for conditions, findings, symptoms, anatomy, and many other clinical ideas.
Concept identifiers help computers distinguish meaning even when users employ different words or synonyms.
Relationships between concepts support organized retrieval and clinical use.
SNOMED CT is suited to detailed clinical documentation rather than broad statistical grouping alone.

slides.title: LOINC standardizes observations and tests
points: LOINC provides standardized identifiers and names for laboratory tests and many clinical observations.
A LOINC concept can describe what was measured, the sample, timing, scale, and sometimes the method.
It helps a receiving system recognize that differently named local tests represent the same observation.
LOINC supports exchange between laboratory information systems and EHRs.
The result value, unit, reference range, and status must still accompany the observation correctly.

slides.title: RxNorm standardizes clinical drug names
points: RxNorm is a standardized terminology for clinical drugs.
It links drug concepts with ingredients, strengths, dose forms, and brand variations.
Standard drug identifiers help systems compare medication information from different sources.
RxNorm can support e-prescribing, pharmacy systems, medication reconciliation, and interaction checking.
It standardizes the drug concept but does not replace clinical judgment or complete prescribing information.

slides.title: Other procedure code sets serve specific uses
points: Procedure code sets describe services, procedures, supplies, or products for defined purposes.
Examples in the source material include CPT and HCPCS in the United States.
Their primary use is often administrative reporting, claims, and reimbursement.
National requirements and code sets differ, so students should focus on the general role of procedure classification.
A code set designed for payment may not provide all the clinical detail needed for patient care.

slides.title: The main standards have distinct roles
points: ICD: classifies diseases and health conditions for reporting and secondary use.
SNOMED CT: represents detailed clinical concepts and relationships.
LOINC: identifies laboratory tests and clinical observations.
RxNorm: identifies standardized clinical drug concepts.
HL7 and FHIR: support the structure and exchange of health information between systems.

slides.title: Exchange standards organize communication
points: Terminology standards help preserve the meaning of individual data elements.
Exchange standards help package those elements into a message, document, or resource.
They define expected structures so sending and receiving systems can process information consistently.
Implementation guides may further specify which elements are required for a particular use case.
Both sides must implement and test the agreed rules for exchange to work reliably.

slides.title: HL7 supports healthcare information exchange
points: Health Level Seven, or HL7, refers to a family of standards for exchanging electronic health information.
HL7 approaches can represent clinical observations, orders, results, documents, and other healthcare information.
Shared models and structures help systems interpret exchanged content consistently.
Different HL7 standards and versions may coexist within healthcare organizations.
HL7 is a standards organization and standards family, not a single software product.

slides.title: FHIR uses reusable healthcare resources
points: Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources, or FHIR, is an HL7 standard for exchanging health information.
FHIR represents information as reusable resources, such as a patient, observation, medication, or encounter.
Resources can be combined to support specific healthcare exchange needs.
FHIR is designed to work with web, mobile, cloud, and EHR environments.
In this course, students need the concept and purpose rather than technical API implementation.

slides.title: FHIR does not replace every older standard
points: Healthcare systems contain many existing interfaces, documents, messages, and workflows.
Organizations may use FHIR alongside earlier HL7 approaches and other standards.
Migration depends on system capability, use case, cost, policy, and partner readiness.
A modern exchange format still requires standardized meaning, accurate data, security, and governance.
Interoperability usually develops through gradual improvement rather than one complete replacement.

slides.title: Semantic interoperability preserves meaning
points: Semantic interoperability means that the receiving system can interpret exchanged information with the intended meaning.
A shared code can identify the same diagnosis, test, observation, or medicine across systems.
The surrounding context—such as unit, date, status, subject, and method—also matters.
Terminologies and classifications support meaning, while exchange standards carry that meaning between systems.
Human review remains important when information is ambiguous, incomplete, or mapped from local data.

slides.title: Mapping connects local and shared codes
points: Organizations often begin with local names and codes created for their own workflows.
Mapping links a local code to a shared terminology or classification.
Mappings can support exchange, reporting, analysis, and transition between classification versions.
One local concept may not always match one standard concept exactly.
Mappings require documentation, validation, version control, maintenance, and expert review.

slides.title: Standards work together in patient care
points: A clinician records a detailed problem using a clinical terminology such as SNOMED CT.
A laboratory identifies an ordered test or result using LOINC.
Medication information can use a standardized drug terminology such as RxNorm.
Relevant conditions may be classified with ICD for reporting and secondary use.
HL7 or FHIR can carry the structured information between the EHR, laboratory, pharmacy, and other systems.

slides.title: Standards improve use but do not remove risk
points: Shared standards support consistency, comparison, automation, reporting, and exchange.
Incorrect code selection can transmit a precise but wrong meaning.
Outdated versions and inconsistent implementation can create mismatches.
Missing context or poor documentation can reduce the usefulness of standardized data.
Governance, training, testing, quality review, and maintenance are necessary throughout the data lifecycle.

slides.title: Choose a standard according to the task
points: Begin with the information need: documentation, exchange, reporting, reimbursement, analysis, or decision support.
Select a terminology or classification that represents the required clinical meaning and level of detail.
Select an exchange standard and implementation rules that both systems support.
Confirm required context, versions, mappings, security, consent, and data-quality checks.
Test the complete workflow with sending users, receiving users, and realistic patient information.

slides.title: Key terms to know
points: HIE: electronic sharing of health information among authorized participants.
HIO: an organization that facilitates or manages health information exchange.
Interoperability: the ability of systems to exchange and meaningfully use information.
Classification: a system that groups related concepts into categories.
Clinical terminology: a structured set of detailed clinical concepts.
Semantic interoperability: preservation of intended meaning across systems.

slides.title: Study questions
points: What is the difference between HIE and an HIO?
Why is connectivity alone insufficient for interoperability?
Give two benefits and two barriers associated with HIE.
Compare centralized and federated exchange.
Distinguish a classification from a clinical terminology.
State the main purpose of ICD, SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm, HL7, and FHIR.
Explain how several standards could work together during one patient encounter.

slides.title: Final summary
points: HIE allows relevant health information to follow patients across authorized care settings.
Interoperability requires connection, shared structure, shared meaning, usable workflow, and trust.
ICD classifies conditions; SNOMED CT represents clinical concepts; LOINC identifies observations; RxNorm identifies drugs.
HL7 and FHIR support structured electronic exchange between healthcare systems.
Standards create a common language, but accurate documentation, governance, privacy, quality, and human judgment remain essential.

weeks.title: Healthcare Data Analytics
weeks.description: The four types of analytics and the analytical workflow.
weeks.arDescription: أنواع التحليلات الأربعة وخطوات تحليل البيانات الصحية.

slides.title: Healthcare Data Analytics, Visualization and Data Quality Weeks 8-9 study deck How healthcare data becomes evidence, insight, and safer decisions
Learning outcomes
points: Explain what healthcare data analytics is and why it supports fact-based decisions.
Distinguish descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics.
Describe the main steps from data collection through preprocessing, modeling, and evaluation.
Explain how data quality and visualization affect interpretation.
Recognize how dashboards and clinical decision support connect information to action.

slides.title: WEEK 8 Healthcare data analytics Focus: how data, information technology, and analysis help healthcare professionals answer questions and make decisions. Study goal: recognize the four types of analytics and describe a simple analytics workflow without doing advanced mathematics.
Data analytics turns evidence into insight
points: Data analytics uses data, information technology, and analysis to gain insight into a problem.
Healthcare analytics can support patient care, operations, quality improvement, and planning.
The same data may answer different questions depending on the purpose of the analysis.
A useful result should be understandable, relevant, timely, and connected to a decision.
Analytics supports judgment; it does not remove the need for professional judgment.

slides.title: Data becomes useful when it is given context
points: Data are basic facts, observations, measurements, words, symbols, images, or numbers.
Information is data that have been processed and interpreted for a purpose.
Context includes who or what was measured, when it was recorded, how it was collected, and why it matters.
A number without a unit, date, subject, or definition can be misleading.
A data dictionary and metadata help explain what a field means and how it should be used.

slides.title: Analytics supports primary and secondary uses
points: Primary use supports direct care for an individual patient.
Secondary use supports activities beyond the immediate encounter.
Examples include quality improvement, research, public-health reporting, planning, and adverse-event detection.
The idea of collect once, use many encourages responsible reuse of reliable healthcare data.
Secondary use still requires attention to purpose, privacy, governance, and data quality.

slides.title: Four types of analytics answer different questions
points: Descriptive analytics asks: What happened?
Diagnostic analytics asks: Why did it happen?
Predictive analytics asks: What might happen next?
Prescriptive analytics asks: What action might be appropriate?
The four types can be used together in one healthcare improvement project.

slides.title: Descriptive analytics summarizes what happened
points: Descriptive analytics reports patterns in existing data.
Examples include the number of admissions, average length of stay, or monthly readmissions.
Counts, percentages, averages, rates, and simple charts are common outputs.
Descriptive results help teams see the current situation before asking why it occurred.
A summary is only useful when the population, timeframe, and definitions are clear.

slides.title: Diagnostic analytics explores why it happened
points: Diagnostic analytics examines relationships, differences, and possible explanations for an observed pattern.
A team might compare readmissions by unit, diagnosis, discharge plan, or time period.
Cross-tabulations, correlations, and exploratory data analysis can reveal useful patterns.
A relationship does not automatically prove that one factor caused another.
Clinicians and analysts should consider workflow, context, and limitations before concluding.

slides.title: Predictive analytics estimates what may happen
points: Predictive analytics uses existing data to estimate a future or unknown outcome.
Examples include identifying patients at risk of readmission or predicting demand for beds.
Predictions are probabilities or estimates, not guarantees.
The quality of a prediction depends on the data, the outcome definition, the population, and the method.
Predictions should be evaluated and used with appropriate clinical and operational context.

slides.title: Prescriptive analytics considers possible actions
points: Prescriptive analytics asks what action could be taken in response to an observed or predicted situation.
A system might suggest follow-up, allocate resources, or prioritize a review.
Recommendations should consider benefits, risks, feasibility, policy, and patient preferences.
A recommendation is not the same as an order or an automatic decision.
Human users remain responsible for deciding whether an action is appropriate.

slides.title: Start with a clear healthcare question
points: State the problem and the decision that the analysis should support.
Define the population, timeframe, outcome, comparison, and important data elements.
Ask whether the available data can answer the question reliably.
Decide how the result will be used and who needs to understand it.
A clear question prevents unnecessary analysis and reduces misinterpretation.

slides.title: The analytics workflow begins with collection
points: Data may come from EHRs, laboratory systems, pharmacy systems, claims, registries, devices, surveys, or research.
Collection should match the purpose of the analysis and the needs of the intended users.
The team should know who enters the data, when it is entered, and which fields are required.
A data warehouse can organize data for reporting and analysis.
A data lake may hold large amounts of varied data for later processing.

slides.title: Preprocessing prepares data for analysis
points: Preprocessing includes understanding the data, cleaning errors, handling missing values, and normalizing formats.
A data dictionary explains field names, definitions, units, valid values, and collection methods.
Duplicate records, impossible values, inconsistent categories, and incorrect dates should be investigated.
Missing data should be described and handled using a documented method.
The goal is not to make the data look perfect; it is to make limitations visible and results trustworthy.

slides.title: Feature engineering creates useful analysis inputs
points: A feature is a data element used to describe a patient, event, or situation in an analysis.
Feature engineering selects, transforms, or combines available data for a defined question.
Examples include converting a date into time since admission or grouping ages into bands.
Clustering and dimensionality-reduction methods can help summarize complex data.
Features should be clinically meaningful, documented, and created without leaking future information.

slides.title: Models learn patterns from prepared data
points: Supervised learning uses examples with known outcomes to predict or classify new cases.
Unsupervised learning searches for patterns or groups without a predefined outcome.
Reinforcement learning learns through feedback from actions and outcomes.
Regression estimates a numeric value; classification assigns a category; clustering forms groups.
Students need to recognize these ideas, not build algorithms for this general course.

slides.title: Evaluation asks whether a model is useful
points: A model should be evaluated before it is used in a healthcare workflow.
For numeric prediction, examples include R-squared, mean squared error, and mean absolute error.
For classification, examples include accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1-score, and AUC.
Different measures answer different questions, so one number is rarely enough.
Evaluation should consider performance, calibration, fairness, usability, and the consequences of errors.

slides.title: Analytics needs context beyond a score
points: A high average performance can hide weak performance for particular groups or settings.
The analysis population should resemble the population in which the result will be used.
Time period, missing data, changing practice, and data drift can affect results.
A result should be checked against clinical knowledge and operational reality.
Transparent limitations help users decide when to trust, question, or not use an output.

slides.title: A readmission example connects the four types
points: Descriptive: readmissions increased from one month to the next.
Diagnostic: the increase is concentrated in two units and a small set of conditions.
Predictive: some patients have higher estimated risk before discharge.
Prescriptive: the team considers follow-up calls or medication review for selected patients.
The final action still depends on clinical review, resources, patient needs, and local policy.

slides.title: What students do not need to calculate here
points: You do not need to derive machine-learning algorithms or implement a programming pipeline.
You do not need to tune models, select hyperparameters, or prove a causal relationship.
You should know what each analytics type is intended to answer.
You should be able to explain a healthcare example and identify important limitations.
You should be able to interpret a simple result responsibly.

slides.title: Responsible analytics keeps people in the loop
points: Analytics should support care and organizational decisions rather than obscure responsibility.
Users need to know what data were used, what the result means, and what it does not mean.
Automated outputs should be reviewed when data are incomplete, unusual, or outside the model's intended setting.
Privacy, security, fairness, and patient impact should be considered before use.
Monitoring after implementation helps identify errors, drift, and unintended consequences.

slides.title: Analytics can guide quality improvement
points: A team can use analytics to identify a gap, investigate its causes, and select a possible intervention.
The team can monitor whether the intervention changes the selected measure over time.
Results should be interpreted alongside workflow changes, staffing, policy, and patient context.
