A measure may improve while another important outcome worsens, so review should be balanced.
Continuous learning connects analytics to practical improvement rather than a one-time report.

slides.title: Key terms to know
points: Data analytics: using data and analysis to gain insight and support decisions.
Descriptive analytics: explains what happened.
Diagnostic analytics: explores why it happened.
Predictive analytics: estimates what may happen.
Prescriptive analytics: considers what action may be appropriate.
Preprocessing: preparing data through understanding, cleaning, missing-data handling, and normalization.

slides.title: Week 8 summary
points: Analytics turns healthcare data into information that can support fact-based decisions.
Descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics answer different questions.
A sound workflow moves from a clear question through collection, preprocessing, feature creation, modeling, and evaluation.
Model performance must be interpreted in context, including limitations and consequences of error.
The appropriate level for BHIM473 is recognition, explanation, example, and responsible interpretation.

weeks.title: Visualization & Data Quality
weeks.description: Data quality, visualization, metadata, dashboards, and decisions.
weeks.arDescription: جودة البيانات والتصور البياني والبيانات الوصفية ولوحات المعلومات.

slides.title: WEEK 9 Visualization, decision support and data quality Focus: how the quality and presentation of data shape what healthcare users see, understand, and do. Study goal: identify common quality problems, choose clear presentations, and connect dashboards to decisions.
Data quality determines whether results can be trusted
points: Data quality describes how well data are fit for their intended use.
Poor data can create incorrect counts, misleading trends, and inappropriate recommendations.
Quality should be considered when data are collected, entered, stored, exchanged, analyzed, and presented.
A data-quality problem may require correction, clarification, exclusion, or a clear limitation statement.
Good analysis cannot fully compensate for data that do not represent the situation accurately.

slides.title: Ask quality questions before using data
points: For what purpose were the data originally collected?
How were the data collected, entered, coded, and changed over time?
Are definitions, units, categories, and standards clear?
Which fields are missing, duplicated, delayed, or implausible?
How will the data be analyzed and presented so that users can interpret them correctly?

slides.title: Accuracy and completeness are basic quality dimensions
points: Accuracy means that a value correctly represents the patient, event, measurement, or condition.
Completeness means that required information is present for the intended use.
An accurate but incomplete record may still lead to an unsafe or biased conclusion.
Examples of missing information include absent allergies, incomplete outcomes, or an unrecorded result.
Quality checks should focus on fields that affect care, reporting, or decisions.

slides.title: Consistency and timeliness matter too
points: Consistency means that the same concept, unit, category, or rule is used in comparable records.
Timeliness means that information is available and current when it is needed.
A delayed result may be accurate but not useful for a time-sensitive decision.
Inconsistent categories can make two departments appear different when they recorded the same event differently.
Quality dimensions should be judged against the purpose and timeframe of the use.

slides.title: Collection choices shape data quality
points: Organizations should decide why data are being entered and which fields are necessary.
The data-entry method should fit the user, setting, workflow, and type of information.
Required fields and controlled values can improve consistency but may reduce flexibility.
Free text can preserve detail but may be harder to search, count, or compare.
Training and feedback help users understand how their documentation affects later use.

slides.title: Structured data are easy to compute
points: Structured data use defined fields, formats, and controlled values.
Examples include a coded diagnosis, a date field, a numeric measurement, or a selected category.
Structured data are easier to query, count, compare, and use in analytics.
Rigid choices can omit nuance or force users to select an imperfect category.
Good design balances computability with the clinical meaning users need to record.

slides.title: Unstructured data preserve narrative detail
points: Unstructured data include narrative notes, free text, images, audio, and other content without a fixed field structure.
Narrative documentation can express context, uncertainty, timing, and patient experience.
It is more difficult to search and analyze directly than structured data.
Natural language processing can help identify concepts, but negation and temporal meaning remain challenging.
Many healthcare environments need both structured fields and meaningful narrative.

slides.title: NLP can make narrative data more usable
points: Natural language processing, or NLP, converts human language into information that computer systems can manipulate.
NLP may help identify diagnoses, symptoms, medications, findings, or public-health signals in narrative text.
It can support patient care, biosurveillance, research, and administrative work.
A system must distinguish whether a concept is present, absent, historical, planned, or uncertain.
NLP outputs should be validated before they are used for important decisions.

slides.title: Metadata explains what data mean
points: Metadata are descriptive details about other data.
Examples include a field definition, unit, source system, collection date, coding system, or version.
Metadata help users understand how data were created and whether they are suitable for a purpose.
They support reliability, quality review, reproducibility, and investigation.
Without metadata, two fields with similar names may be incorrectly treated as equivalent.

slides.title: Cleaning identifies errors and unusual values
points: Data cleaning checks for impossible, inconsistent, duplicated, or incorrectly coded values.
Descriptive statistics can reveal unusual ranges, extreme values, and unexpected distributions.
Crosstabs can show patterns that suggest a data-entry or coding problem.
The correct value should be verified from a reliable source when possible.
If an error cannot be corrected, the decision to exclude or retain the record should be documented.

slides.title: Missing data require a documented decision
points: Missingness may occur because a field was not asked, not known, not applicable, or not entered.
Removing records can reduce the sample and may introduce bias.
A coded value for missing data should not be mistaken for a real measurement.
Imputation replaces a missing value using a defined rule, such as a median or another model-based estimate.
The chosen approach and its possible effect on results should be reported.

slides.title: Descriptive checks help find quality problems
points: Counts and percentages can reveal unexpected categories or large amounts of missing data.
Means, medians, ranges, and distributions can reveal implausible continuous values.
Crosstabs compare categories and can identify inconsistent combinations.
A review of merged data should check new fields, derived values, timeframes, and changing definitions.
Analysts should ask whether counts, sums, and averages make sense in the clinical setting.

slides.title: Visualization helps users see patterns
points: A visualization can show the shape of data, trends, skew, outliers, and missing information.
Charts can make comparisons easier than a long list of numbers.
A visualization should answer a defined question rather than decorate the data.
Labels, units, timeframes, denominators, and sources help users interpret the display.
The same data can support different conclusions when the scale or grouping is changed.

slides.title: Choose a chart that fits the question
points: Use a bar chart to compare categories or groups.
Use a line chart to show change over time.
Use a histogram to show the distribution of a numeric variable.
Use a table when exact values or several related fields must be read together.
Use a text summary when one clear sentence communicates the result better than a graphic.

slides.title: Clear visuals avoid distortion
points: The visual size of a number or percentage should be proportional to the quantity represented.
Axes should be labeled clearly and scaled honestly.
Abbreviations should be explained when they may confuse the audience.
Color should support meaning and remain understandable when printed or viewed by people with color- vision differences.
Text, capitalization, and font size should make the chart easy to read.

slides.title: Tables should stand on their own
points: A table should be a logical unit that a reader can understand without searching elsewhere.
The title, row headings, column headings, units, and timeframe should be understandable.
The source of the data should be identified.
Blank cells should be distinguished from zero, not applicable, or missing values.
Consistent formatting helps readers compare cells without confusion.

slides.title: Exploratory analysis checks whether the story makes sense
points: Exploratory data analysis combines descriptive statistics, relationships, and visualization.
It helps analysts understand the data before applying more formal methods.
After merging data, review new variables, derived values, timeframes, and values that may change over time.
Check whether the analysis is correct and whether the outputs are plausible.
Exploration can reveal questions that require better data or a revised analysis plan.

slides.title: Dashboards connect information to action
points: A dashboard brings selected measures together so users can monitor a situation.
A useful dashboard shows the right information to the right people in a form they can understand.
Users need definitions, timeframes, comparison points, and alerts that support a real workflow.
Too many measures, unclear scales, or low-quality data can distract or mislead.
A dashboard should lead to a question, review, or action—not replace thinking.

slides.title: Decision support uses information at the right moment
points: Clinical decision support provides patient-specific or situation-specific information to support a healthcare decision.
Examples include medication warnings, preventive-care reminders, order guidance, and prompts for missing information.
The five rights are the right information, person, format, channel, and time.
Decision support works better when data are accurate, relevant, and integrated into workflow.
Users must interpret the information and decide what action is appropriate.

slides.title: Big data increases both opportunity and responsibility
points: Big data is often described by high volume, high velocity, and high variety.
Healthcare data may combine records, claims, devices, registries, images, and other sources.
More data do not automatically mean better evidence.
Different sources may use different definitions, populations, timeframes, and quality controls.
Large-scale analysis requires careful governance, documentation, privacy protection, and validation.

slides.title: Key terms to know
points: Data quality: how well data fit their intended use.
Accuracy: whether a value correctly represents what it describes.
Completeness: whether required information is present.
Consistency: whether comparable data use compatible definitions and formats.
Timeliness: whether information is available and current when needed.
Visualization: a purposeful display that helps users interpret data.

slides.title: Study questions
points: What is the difference between data and information?
Distinguish descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics.
What are the main steps in a healthcare analytics workflow?
Why do accuracy, completeness, consistency, and timeliness matter?
Compare structured and unstructured data, including one strength and one limitation of each.
How can a visualization or dashboard help a healthcare user make a decision?
What are the five rights of clinical decision support?

slides.title: Final summary
points: Healthcare analytics turns data into information that can support care, operations, quality, and planning.
The four analytics types answer different questions: what happened, why, what may happen, and what action may help.
Data quality and metadata determine whether an analysis is meaningful and trustworthy.
Clear visualizations and dashboards help users see patterns and connect information to decisions.
Decision support is most useful when it is accurate, timely, understandable, and reviewed by responsible professionals.
